newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Mobile sales add punch to Ericsson.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mobile sales add punch to Ericsson.

text.p: Sweden's AB LM Ericsson, the latest head-turner in the mobile telephone industry, delivered surprisingly good first-half results on Thursday, boosted by a sharp advance in sales of mobile handsets.

The company said pre-tax profit soared 44 percent to 6.10 billion crowns ($781.3 million) in the first half of 1997, more than one billion crowns higher than the market consensus. A weaker Swedish crown boosted the result by about 500 million crowns.
Analysts said handset sales were the icing on the cake.
"They sold around one million more handsets in the second quarter than expected," one analyst said.
Besides healthy growth figures for turnover and order intake, which rose 44 percent and 39 percent respectively, Ericsson said mobile telephone sales rocketed more than 100 percent in the period.
Several said they would be increasing 1997 forecasts.
"The sales were about 10 percent better than we expected. We will probably raise our EPS estimates by about 10 percent for 1997," said Lehman Brothers analyst Jeremy Alun-Jones.
Net sales for the group amounted to 72.21 billion crowns in the period. Its mobile telephones unit posted sales of 18.39 billion crowns compared to 9.09 billion in the six-month period.
Ericsson's result puts it in a league with U.S. rival Motorola Inc., whose better-than-expected profits for the second quarter earlier this month pushed its shares to a two-year high.
Now all eyes are on Finland's Nokia Oy, which reports first-half earnings on August 4. Analysts said they would re-think second quarter estimates in light of Ericsson's result.

Nokia had been expected to show lower mobile phones sales growth than in the first quarter, but analysts say Ericsson's report introduced hopes that second-quarter growth would be closer to the 58 percent reached in the first.

Some analysts, however, raised concerns about Ericsson's increased exposure to the volatile mobile handset market. Ericsson was once set apart from its competitors because of its mobile telephone structure operations.
Ericsson has said it cornered about 40 percent of the mobile infrastructure market, which accounted for 42 percent of the group's total sales in the first half of the year.
Thanks to this, and its traditional public telecoms operations called Infocom Systems, Ericsson could have been better insulated from inevitable falling prices on mobile handsets, analysts said.
"Ericsson is becoming more similar to companies like Nokia as it becomes more dependent on mobile phones than (mobile) systems," said Aros Securities chief analyst Lars Larsen
"It means Ericsson will be more exposed to a consumer market which is more affected by price pressure than systems is and where you can't expect the same margins as in systems."
"You have to consider if this will effect the way you value the company," Larsen added.

Ericsson said gross margins had fallen somewhat in the first half of the year, to 41.9 percent compared to 42.6 percent in 1996 after adjustments for new accounting principles, because of price pressure and changes in product mix.
In theory they could fall more if the high growth rate for sales of mobile handsets continued, Ericsson said.
Finnish rival Nokia said in April it expected handset prices to fall 15-20 percent on average this year.
But Ericsson chief executive Lars Ramqvist did not rain on the parade on Thursday, saying mobile telephone prices had been surpisingly stable.
Ericsson also said it was immune from some price pressure because the market was willing to pay more for its high-end, high-quality products.
One analyst pointed out this tonic only masks inevitable price erosion and said his long-term view for the company was unchanged although his short-term view was more bullish.
"They are enjoying a window of opportunity. It's not a question of if prices will fall, but when," the analyst said.
